帕薩迪納

去年，帕薩迪納租戶正義聯盟一直致力於在 11 月的投票中採取實質性的租金控制措施（帕薩迪納公平和公平住房憲章修正案）。

帕薩迪納的租金創下歷史新高，帕薩迪納市議會最近投票決定從 6 月 30 日開始停止新冠病毒暫停驅逐。該法令要求租戶在暫停結束後六個月內償還任何拖欠的租金。 帕薩迪納一居室公寓的租金中位數為 2,195 美元，這意味著在長達兩年的疫情期間，無法支付全部租金的租戶有可能需要支付數萬美元，或於2023 年 1 月 1 日面臨驅逐 。

僅在過去一個月裡，帕薩迪納一室公寓的平均租金就超過了單間臥室的租金，漲幅達到驚人的 39% 至 2,348 美元。

市議員第3選區: 布蘭登·D·拉馬爾

帕薩迪納人際關係委員會主席布蘭登·D·拉馬爾 (Brandon D. Lamar) 是一名長期居民，他積極參與多項青年計劃。 拉馬爾還擔任帕薩迪納全國有色人種協進會董事會成員，並與帕薩迪納組織進步和領導帕薩迪納合作。

拉馬爾正在開展一項旨在控制租金和經濟適用房、公共安全責任和工人權利的運動。 去年，拉馬爾一直在與帕薩迪納租戶正義聯盟進行拉票，以在選票上獲得租金控制措施，並將成為理事會中唯一的租戶。

現任約翰·肯尼迪 (John Kennedy) 主張創建民警監督委員會，但收到了橙縣房地產利益集團（ARC Investments 和 EverElite Realty）和 Panoptic Development 首席執行官 Jason Wang 的捐款，該公司在帕薩迪納周圍建造了幾個豪華住宅單位。

肯尼迪向租金管制組織者強調說，他認為他們與公共利益律師一起編寫的租金管制措施是“有缺陷的”，儘管他沒有說明原因。 根據他提交的表格 700 ，他的主要業務是房地產投資和諮詢。 他擁有四處房產，其中兩處有租戶。

市議員第5選區:傑西·里瓦斯

現任傑西·里瓦斯（Jess Rivas）無人反對。 她支持租金控制，對取消競選捐款限制投了唯一的一票，並倡導可再生能源。

市議員第7選區: 傑森·里昂

規劃專員傑森·里昂 (Jason Lyon) 支持租金管制運動，並倡導為無家者提供長期住房。 他支持現行的工資協議和工人的組織權，並希望有更多的自行車道。 他認為“我們仍有工作要做，以保護公眾、保障警員安全，並建立無偏見的警務體系。” 他支持警察監督條例。

帕薩迪納西北專員艾倫·謝伊 (Allen Shay) 是帕薩迪納房地產經紀人協會地方政府關係委員會成員。 謝伊批評了槍擊安東尼麥克萊恩 Anthony McClain 和地方檢察官佐治·賈思森決定，不指控帕薩迪納警察埃德溫杜馬金丁(Edwin Dumaguindin) 在背後射殺麥克萊恩。

前規劃專員西蘭·哈建 (Ciran Hadjian) 提出空置管制。 雖然這項立法可以減緩飛漲的住房成本，但空置管制是州科斯塔霍金斯法案阻止城市做的事情。

那麼，為什麼哈建不像里昂那樣支持帕薩迪納公平和公平住房憲章修正案呢？ 哈建還主張建立更多的鄰里監視團體，但研究表明，這些團體不會阻止犯罪並增加對少數族裔的攻擊。

帕薩迪納社區學院區

在現任者的領導下，帕薩迪納城市學院 (PCC) 在國家認證機構將學院置於留校察看期間幾乎失去了認證。 教師對大學校長和董事會投了不信任票。

學生們也投了不信任票。 雖然 PCC 喜歡談論學生平等，但它的行動卻相反，因為它忽略了教師的社會經濟平等和膽量職業課程，包括平面設計和以英語為第二語言 (ESL)，這對有色人種學生很重要。

董事會第三區: 史蒂夫·吉布森

史蒂夫·吉布森 (Steve Gibson) 博士畢業於 PCC，然後獲得教育博士學位。 他寫了一篇關於主要依賴兼職教師提供廉價勞動力的系統的不公正性的論文，這是教師想要解決的 PCC 問題之一。

吉布森是美國朋友服務委員會 (American Friends Service Committee)、伯尼桑德斯運動的主要組織者，並支持其他事業，如「黑人的命也是命 」、租金控制和全民醫療保險。 他得到了Progressive Asian Network for Action的認可。

與現任柏林達·布朗 (Berlinda Brown)競爭，吉布森希望扭轉 PCC 職業教育的穩步減少，降低公司化和高昂的教育成本，提高董事會和行政部門的問責制和透明度，並提升教職員工的聲音，使其成為領導中的平等夥伴 . 他是一個不受企業限制的候選人，得到了教師工會和眾多教授的認可。

董事會第五區: 克莉絲汀鄺

與現任琳達·華 (Linda Wah) 競爭的，克莉絲汀·鄺 (Kristine Kwong) 是一名教育律師，她希望恢復董事會的問責制並改善 PCC 的學術氛圍，將其恢復到曾經的優質教育機構。

教師協會主席 Mark Whitworth 指出：“鄺致力於開放和透明的政府，再加上她的專業知識，將為 PCC 的董事會帶來急切的開放思想。 長期以來，學區一直拒絕聆聽校園和社區利益相關者的聲音，包括我們的教職員工。 教師協會相信克莉絲汀鄺將提高教育質量，為帕薩迪納城市學院的學生、教職員工和整個社區服務。”

董事會第七區: 奧爾頓·王

奧爾頓·王 (Alton Wang) 正在挑戰現任安東尼·費勞 (Anthony Fellow)。 王倡導選民權利和善政。 他是第二代阿卡迪亞人，就讀於公立學校。

羅斯米德

市議員 （投不超過3票）: 喬安妮·羅素·查韋斯

三位現任議員——瑪格麗特·“瑪吉”·克拉克 (Margaret “Maggie” Clark)、桑德拉·阿門塔 (Sandra Armenta) 和史蒂文·李 (Steven Ly)——都投票支持了一項對洛杉磯縣新的改革地區檢察官佐治·賈思森的不信任決議。 李推動了它，克拉克也強烈支持它，雖然阿門塔聲稱需要“平衡”，但她仍然投了贊成票。

此外，克拉克和李都不是組織反對在該市開設沃爾瑪商店的生活工資倡導者的支持者。

挑戰者喬安妮·羅素·查韋斯 Joanne Russell Chavez 是阿罕布拉聯合學區的董事。 雖然她沒有詳細描述她的政策觀點，並且她支持一些反對村莊的項目，因為他們想要更多經濟適用房單位，並且擔心受污染的土壤，但 Knock LA 認為投票反對對賈思森司法改革的現任者很重要，因為這反映了他們對自己警察的政策和缺乏監督。

托倫斯

市​長：克里夫·紐馬克

克里夫·紐馬克 (Cliff Numark) 是托倫斯本地人，他當選為市議會和埃爾卡密諾城市學院理事會成員。 他反對召回佐治·賈思森，但不同意賈思森的改革。

他希望防止來自托倫斯煉油廠的危險，例如致命的改性氫氟酸 (MHF) 的替代品，它可以形成致命的低窪雲，如果洩漏可以殺死數千人。 他希望消防部門監控煉油廠。 他亦希望讓托倫斯更適合步行，並增加負擔得起的、適合住房。

另一位候選人喬治·陳 (George Chen) 是對賈思森進行不信任投票，並支持罷免。 他花了上千美元在市政廳掛上了一個宗教短語，並投票決定殺死土狼，儘管該市有一個有效的驅霧土狼計劃是不需要獵殺。 他還支持一項“反露營”法令，以引証和逮捕無家者。

市財​政​官: 蒂姆·古德里奇

蒂姆·古德里奇 (Tim Goodrich)是一名空軍退伍軍人，他是共同創立了伊拉克退伍軍人反戰組織。 他引用了他作為議員的經驗及於保險公司風險經理的資格。 他提議更換煉油廠中致命的 MHF 酸以安全的替代品代替。 作為一名改革人士，他支持增加 0.5 美分的銷售稅和支持佐治·賈思森競選地區檢察官。

現任達納·科爾特斯 (Dana Cortez) 很少出現在她當選的職位，理由是未公開的醫療狀況。 挑戰者 G·里克·馬歇爾 (G. Rick Marshall) 想要撤回她，反對提高銷售稅。他亦是一個政治行動委員會的成員，該委員會被指控製作性別歧視、種族主義的政治廣告。

另一位候選人邁克·格里菲斯 (Mike Griffiths) 是一位保守的議員和前首席財務官，他反對稅收並支持撤回賈思森。 梅麗莎·M·瑞特 (Melissa M. Wright) 和古德里奇一樣，支持提高銷售稅，儘管很不情願。

市議員第一區: 吉米·高

幾個環保組織支持吉米·高 (Jimmy Gow) 擔任這個開放席位。 與高一樣，大衛·M·卡索尼斯 (David Kartsonis) 也希望煉油廠取代 MHF。 房地產經紀公司總裁喬恩·卡吉 (Jon Kaji) 也表示他反對 MHF，但在最近的一次論壇上提到，他認為警察保護托倫斯居民，儘管州正在調查該部隊的懷偏見短訊。 戴夫·齊吉爾鮑姆 (Dave Zygielbaum) 是警察工會認可的檢察官。

市議員第三區: 阿蕯姆·謝赫

這是另一個空位。阿蕯姆·謝赫 (Asam Sheikh) 想要取代煉油廠的 MHF，並要求警察接受廣泛的培訓，尤其是關於多樣性的培訓。他正在與勞倫·科特納 (Lauren Cotner) 競爭， 保守派議員奧雷利奧·馬圖奇 (Aurelio Mattucci) 的支持者。。

市議員第五區: H·珍·阿德斯曼

H·珍·阿德斯曼 (H. Jean Adelsman) 支持提高銷售稅。 她說監禁無家者是“無情的”，並呼籲在煉油廠更換 MHF。

現任奧雷利奧·馬圖奇 (Aurelio Mattucci) 是臭名昭著的反移民前亞利桑那州警長喬·阿爾帕約 (Joe Arpaio) 的支持者。 馬圖奇反對提高銷售稅，反對向煉油廠施壓停止使用 MHF，並支持撤回賈思森和誘捕土狼。 馬圖奇支持 喬治·陳、邁克·格里菲斯和勞倫·科特納等候選人。

議案 SST (銷售稅): 贊成

加利福尼亞州立法機關

這又經歷一年的疫情，但立法機關未能通過單一支付人的全民醫療保險（CalCare），根據《埃利斯法案》限制房東驅逐，或採取任何新的行動來應對氣候變化。 儘管在兩院都擁有絕對多數，但民主黨在解決該州最緊迫的問題方面仍然令人失望，而是繼續支持州強大的石油和天然氣、健康保險和房地產行業。

不要投票給現任者，除非他們至少支持 CalCare 和 Ellis Act 改革。 即使他們有看似有改革的投票記錄，立法分數也並不總是能說明全部情況。 有時立法者通過修改或阻止委員會聽證會導致法案死亡。 關注資金，看看誰為他們的活動做出了貢獻。

加利福尼亞州參議院

參議院第20選區: 卡羅琳·門吉瓦爾

卡羅琳·門吉瓦爾 (Caroline Menjivar) 開展的競選運動，以增加獲得心理健康和其他支持服務的機會，並關閉懷特曼機場 (Whiteman Airport) 以緩解聖費爾南多谷 (San Fernando Valley) 的污染和噪音問題，該谷共有三個機場。

但她肯定不是一個理想的人選。門吉瓦爾支持將微型住宅作為解決住房和無家者危機的方法。微型住宅只不過是比棚屋較好一點點，微型住宅要求住戶嚴格遵守的行為準則，例如晚上 7:00 的宵禁和幾乎不存在的訪客窗口。

然而，反對者丹尼爾·赫茨伯格 (Daniel Hertzberg) 也支持“加倍投資”在微型住宅，並且似乎通過他的父親、前議長鮑勃赫茨伯格 (Bob Hertzberg)（順便說一下，他喜歡從石油行業那裡拿錢）獲得了大部分資金和支持）。 事實上，小赫茨伯格的競選網站“遇見丹尼爾” 30%部分的是由大赫茨伯格提供。在剩下的候選人中， 伊利·德拉克魯茲·阿亞奧 (Ely De La Cruz Ayao) 是一位”反對選擇”的房地產經紀人。賽廸·亞曆杭德拉·莫拉萊斯 (Seydi Alejandra Morales) 似乎有一些很好的政策建議，但似乎缺乏基層的改革支持。

州參議院第22選區: 無建議

州參議院第24選區: 本·艾倫

參議員本·艾倫 (Ben Allen)的投票記錄一直是立法機關中最改革的記錄之一，儘管民主黨擁有 75% 的絕對多數，但該記錄的表現卻大大低於選民的預期。 艾倫是參議院憲法修正案 2 的作者，該修正案將廢除在州憲法中增加的一項要求（在反對公民權利的強烈反對期間），即每個新的公共住房建設項目都必須進行投票並得到選民的批准。

不幸的是，即使是立法機構中的民主黨人，他也無法獲得足夠的支持來推動法案向前發展。 在環境問題上，他也是一個可靠的盟友。 他沒有競爭對手，但即便如此，他也值得你投票。

注：艾倫在舊區界線下於 2020 年為第26選​區當選。在2021 年，加州根據 2020 年人口普查重新劃分了立法區。 本指南中的地區編號反映了今年的選票內容。

州參議院第28選區: 蘿拉·斯莫爾伍德-庫瓦斯

蘿拉·斯莫爾伍德-庫瓦斯 (Lola Smallwood-Cuevas) 是一位經驗豐富的勞工領袖，也是洛杉磯黑人工人中心的創始人。 儘管開展了一場安靜的競選活動，斯莫爾伍德-庫瓦斯已經籌集了超過26萬美元，主要來自工會。 斯莫爾伍德-庫瓦斯是一名有效的政治人物，還獲得了 SEIU California 等許多強大工會和州參議員悉尼·卡姆拉格 (Sydney Kamlager) 等有影響力的民選官員的支持。

斯莫爾伍德-庫瓦斯似乎是少數有意利用她的人脈為善的內部人士之一。 她正在開展一項支持勞工、公共房居和全民醫療保健的運動，此外她還支持關閉英格爾伍德油田。

至於其他候選人，賈馬爾·A·古爾利奇 (Jamaal Gulledge) 在這些問題上與斯莫爾伍德-庫瓦斯相似，但缺乏機構支持，卡米拉·維多利亞·摩爾 (Kamilah Victoria Moore) 是一名賠償律師和倡導者（這很好），但在其他問題上似乎沒有任何直言不諱的立場，謝麗爾·C·特納 (Cheryl Turner) 對住房和無家者問題的解決方案有著經典的新自由主義態度，例如促進密度獎金和向私人開發商提供稅收優惠，而喬·利蘇佐 (Joe Lisuzzo) 則支持增加警察支出。

州參議院第30選區: 瑪莎·卡馬喬·羅德裏格斯

現任鮑勃·阿丘利塔 (Bob Archuleta) 是一名前傘兵和警察，在代表洛杉磯東南部縣區的四年中，他所做的很少。 他發起的大多數法案都是相對安全的美德信號行為——例如正式承認週年紀念日和具有重要文化意義的日期的法案。 他拒絕支持《氣候危機法案》，以及一項允許解除警察執照的法案，這是 Knock LA 的首要任務。

值得注意的是，2021 年 3 月，一位前匿名工作人員指控阿丘利塔進行性騷擾，包括聲稱不受歡迎的求愛。 該訴訟還指控阿丘利塔因提出疑慮和違反其他勞動法而對前僱員進行報復。

Knock LA 建議投票給草根組織者瑪莎·卡馬喬·羅德裏格斯，或惠蒂爾市議員亨利·布喬特 (Henry Bouchot)。 羅德裏格斯是一位水資源倡導者，曾在恢復三角洲、食品與水觀察、塞拉俱樂部和 Dignity and Power Now 等組織中發揮積極作用。 她還是中央盆地市水區第一部的當選主任。

布喬特是前現役海軍陸戰隊法官倡導者和阿富汗退伍軍人，他創立了非營利組織 Praccess，為殘疾退伍軍人提供服務，特別是在 Skid Row。 根據布喬特的競選網站，他沒有從特殊利益集團那裡拿錢，他的首要任務是經濟適用房，以真正的解決方案和同理心去解決無家者危機、保護環境和可負擔的醫療保健。 在描述他在惠蒂爾市議會任職時，布喬特告訴《惠蒂爾每日新聞》，“四年時間足以讓我完成我打算做的事情，甚至更多。” 要是阿丘利塔也能這麼說就好了。

這場選舉中唯一的共和黨人米奇·克萊蒙斯擁有自己的管道公司，根據選民邊緣Voter’s Edge的問卷調查，他認為“罪案已經失控”，並承諾“恢復我們社區的法律和秩序”。

注：阿丘萊特在舊區界線下於 2020 年為第32選​區當選。在2021 年，加州根據 2020 年人口普查重新劃分了立法區。 本指南中的地區編號反映了今年的選票內容。

州​眾​議​院第 39 選​區: 胡安·卡裏略

第 39 選​區是一個新創建的地區，覆蓋蘭開斯特、帕姆代爾和洛杉磯湖，沒有現職者。 前帕姆代爾學校董事會成員和現任帕姆代爾市議員胡安·卡裏略 (Juan Carrillo) 是候選人中的最佳選擇。

當帕姆代爾市議會最近對洛杉磯縣地方檢察官佐治·賈思森進行不信任投票時，卡裏略投下了唯一的反對票。 他投票反對帕姆代爾市發起一項對起訴犯罪本身的研究（而不是洛杉磯地區檢察官辦公室），稱“這筆錢最好用在其他地方以防止犯罪，而不是資助一個新的市政府部門。”

克里斯蒂·史密斯 (Christy Smith) 的前政治主任，安德裏亞·羅森塔爾 (Andrea Rosenthal) 顯然是民主黨願意選擇的人選，她得到了著名自由民主黨人的支持和大多數工會的競選捐款，但她主張“確保優質的全民可負擔的醫療保健和住房”，這是不支持全民醫療保險的雙重說法。 議會肯定會在下個任期內就另一項單一支付者醫療衛生法案進行投票，不支持通過該法案的候選人不應獲得支持。

在 2014 年湯姆·拉基（Tom Lackey）將他趕下台後，前加利福尼亞州議員史蒂夫·G·福克斯（Steve Fox）在幾次試圖返回薩克拉門托 (Sacramento) 失敗後，也在競選這個席位。福克斯被指控性騷擾一名女僱員，以及強迫另一名州僱員為他的律師事務所無酬工作。 加州以 21萬美元和解了這兩件案件。 福克斯在本週期最值得注意的競選問題是一項新的封建主義住房政策，可以為無家者提供微型房屋，並通過為州改善道路來支付房租。

州​眾​議​院​第 40 選​區: 皮拉爾·夏沃

第 40 選​區有三名候選人在競選，沒有人能像皮拉爾·夏沃(Pilar Schiavo) 那樣出色。 夏沃推行的競選策劃是一個公共教育資金、精神保健支援和保證每個人的醫療保健的平台。

夏沃是一位經驗豐富的勞工組織者，明確支持單一支付者醫療法案 AB1400，並得到議員李天明 (Alex Lee) 的支持。

現任蘇賽特·馬丁內斯·瓦拉達雷斯 (Suzette Valladares)是一名共和黨人，他反對全民醫療保護。另一位亦在競選這個席位的還有安妮·E·趙 (Annie Cho)。

州​眾​議​院​第 46 選​區: 傑西·加布裏埃爾

議員傑西·加布裏埃爾 (Jesse Gabriel) 是一位遵循選民和倡導者反饋意見的立法者。 在之前的選舉中，Knock LA 沒有推薦他，因為他沒有公開承諾支持“黑人的命也是命”——洛杉磯的首要任務：讓加利福尼亞——像其他 46 個州一樣——為警察的違法行為吊銷其執法資格。

臭名遠播的議會議長安東尼·倫登（Anthony Rendon）引用了一個事實，即只有不到一半的議會公開承諾支持它，這是他沒有在 2020 年將其付諸表決的原因。加布裏埃爾的辦公室在該選民指南公佈後聯繫了 Knock LA， 解釋說他打算投票給它。 加布裏埃爾不僅在 2021 年投票支持它，他還投票支持其他改革優先事項，例如全民醫療保險 / CalCare。

加布裏埃爾唯一的對手是退休校長達娜卡魯索 (Dana Caruso)，她想“把駐校警察帶回我們的學校”。 Knock LA 以高標準要求民選官員，因此 Knock LA 感謝像議員加布里埃爾這樣的人堅持到底。

州​眾​議​院​第 51 選​區: 路易·阿布拉姆森

新的第 51 選​區覆蓋聖莫尼卡、西洛杉磯、比佛利山莊、西好萊塢、好萊塢山、好萊塢和漢考克公園，是洛杉磯最好的富人區之一。

路易·阿布拉姆森 (Louis Abramson) 是中央好萊塢社區委員會的成員，並且是一名天體物理學家。 雖然他籌集的 $120,709 美元，與對手裏克·查韋斯·茨布爾 (Rick Zbur) 的收入相差無幾，但他的貢獻主要來自個人，而且他沒有從警察協會、保險公司、能源公司或特許學校獲得任何資金。

阿布拉姆森是一名租戶，這是一個罕見的區別，因為從市政到聯邦的各級民選官員中，超過 80% 是房主，超過四分之一的加利福尼亞州立法機構成員也是房東。

到目前為止，茨布爾已經籌集了令人瞠目結舌的 $814,505.62 美元的競選捐款，其中一筆來自一家名為 GTM Group Holdings 的控股公司，該公司被描述為“專注於最大限度地提高客戶銷售產品能力的銷售諮詢和政府採購公司， 為聯邦和 SLED 市場（州、地方、教育）提供服務和解決方案。” 這聽起來像極一個人才中介，發掘政府官員去行賄以代表集團公司。茨布爾還從特斯拉、特許學校、能源公司和保險公司那裡獲得資金。

州​眾​議​院​第 52 選​區: 米婭·利瓦斯·波特

第 52 選​區覆蓋了 NELA、洛斯費利茲、銀湖、格倫代爾和東洛杉磯的大部分地區。 它是洛杉磯最改革的選區，沒有之一，並且應該有一位合法地反映其選民的候選人。

米婭·利瓦斯·波特 (Mia Livas Porter) 一直是 Moms Demand Action 和 Everytown for Gun Safety 的組織者，在她哥哥與精神分裂症長期鬥爭後自殺身亡之後，致力於預防槍支暴力。 她在教師罷工期間支持 UTLA，並正為加州推行綠色新政、單一支付者醫療保健，並通過對經濟適用房、教育、醫療保健和公共交通的再投資來重新構想公共安全。 波特沒有從警察協會、保險公司、醫療或製藥公司、特許學校或能源公司那裡拿走任何錢。

民主黨現任議員溫迪·卡裏略 (Wendy Carrillo) ，在 2017 年以伯尼克拉特（Berniecrat）的名義當選時，令她所在選區的改革人士感到失望。 對於任何聲稱在公職中與桑德斯 (Sanders) 一起抗爭的人來說，她在獲勝後最初對全民醫療保險的胡扯是不可接受的。 儘管卡裏略從那時起就共同贊助了 CalCare 法案並贏得了全國護士聯合會的支持，但她以三倍的金錢贊助超過波特，通過從健康保險公司、警察協會、特許學校和能源公司獲得資金。

共和黨人賈·達馬托 (Gia D’Amato) 是一名右翼保守派基督徒，以反共和反疫苗的身份參選，也參加了這場競選。

如果您住在威尼斯、英格爾伍德和朗代爾之間，您的選票上的兩場選戰可能會令人困惑。 除了新61區的常規初選外，舊62區還有一個特別的決選來結束當前任期，該區與新61區大部分重疊，目前空缺。

這意味著來自第 62 區的兩名決選候選人——蒂娜·西蒙娜·麥金納 (Tina Simone McKinnor) 和現任朗代爾市長羅伯特·普倫-邁爾斯 (Robert Pullen-Miles) ——如果您在新的重疊區域，可能會在您的選票上出現兩次。

早在 2 月份，議員奥特姆‧伯克 (Autumn Burke) 就辭去了她的職務。 她加入了 Axiom Advisors，這是一家由說客創立的遊說公司，儘管有新冠病毒的限制，她還是在 2020 年與州長加文·紐森在法國洗衣房餐廳共進晚餐。 正因為如此，62 區在 4 月 5 日舉行了一次特別初選，而普倫-邁爾斯現在正在與麥金納進行決選。

蒂娜·西蒙娜·麥金納 (Tina McKinnor) 是一位長期的活動家和本土人洛杉磯人，她是 LA Voice 的公民參與總監，這是一個“致力於為所有人提供平等和富足的多種族、多信仰、以社區為基礎的組織”。 她得到了Ground Game LA的認可。

麥金納支持單一支付者醫療衛生系統，以及更強大的租戶權利和免遭驅逐的保護。 她的首要任務還包括新冠病毒恢復、解決非法短期租賃和住房危機、減少被監禁人數，同時還提供幫助以前被監禁的人重新進入社會的計劃。

普倫-邁爾斯在他的競選網站上列出了類似的目標，例如新冠病毒救濟、無家者政策、環境保護和婚姻平等。 然而，一些措施，比如他在 2020 年 4 月通過阻止使用當地酒店為 Project Roomkey來取悅 (鄰避症候群)NIMBY所做的努力一樣，改革人士的擔憂是可以理解的。這與麥金納在當地組織和政策方面的記錄相比，是 Knock LA 推薦麥金納的原因。

拉哈布拉市議員羅斯·埃斯皮諾薩 (Rose Espinoza)說，她“支持墮胎，當手術對母親的生命和健康是必要的時條”，這不是贊成的”支持選擇”。

羅伯特·羅伯·坎西奧（Robert Cancio）是一名退伍軍人，他說他“打擊犯罪”並呼籲在州內進行更多的石油鑽探。勞爾·奧爾蒂斯·JR (Raul Ortiz) 支持警察，反對墮胎權和新冠病毒疫苗。投阿爾坎塔是明智的選擇。

州​眾​議​院​第 65 選​區: 法蒂瑪·伊克巴爾·祖貝爾

她是瓦茨的一名教師、移民、社區組織者和有特殊需要的兒子的母親。 她在推行一個強大的交叉平台，並且她已經在她想要領導的問題上表現出領導力：包括環境正義、公共教育投資、刑事司法改革、經濟適用房和經濟平等。

她的對手，議員邁克·安東尼·吉普森（Mike Gipson）在議會中取得了最多的企業資金，而該地區——以及我們的州——正在為此買單。 吉普森一次又一次地表現出為社區的捐助者服務。

吉普森最近在視頻中被問及他糟糕的氣候記錄和跟化石燃料的關係，他激怒了一位年輕的社區成員。 之後，在仇外回應中，他將法蒂瑪斥為“不是來自這個國家”。

吉普森也是一名前警官，面對喬治·弗洛伊德起義(George Floyd Uprisings)，他只支持最薄弱的執法改革。

州​眾​議​院​第 69 選​區: 無建議

美國國會

在新冠肺炎疫情的兩年中，國會尚未通過全民聯邦醫療保險。 事實上，國會在這個任期內甚至都沒有投票過。 雖然來自洛杉磯的幾位國會議員將他們的名字添加到了全民醫療保險的共同贊助者名單中 – 朝著正確方向邁出了一小步 – 他們每個人都在 3 月份投票支持取消單一付款人醫療保健資金的綜合法案，我們進行了：新冠病毒測試、疫苗接種和未投保人治療覆蓋。

因此，儘管有幾名國會議員上次Knock LA推薦，例如代表格蕾絲·納波利塔諾 (Grace Napolitano)，趙美心 (Judy Chu)，瑪克辛·沃特斯 (Maxine Waters) 和納內特-迪亞斯-巴拉甘 (Nanette Barragán)，他們的投票記錄通常不令人反感，但Knock LA 強調了全民醫療保險的緊迫性，不推薦任何投票支持綜合法案的現任總統。

是的，《綜合法案》涵蓋了很多東西，包括超過3700億美元的軍事和武器支出，這使得在 100 萬美國人死亡後，無法為新冠疫情提供 150 億美元的資金醫療覆蓋。

注意：此席位在選票上兩次出現：

  1. 第一個是從2023年1月3日開始的“完整任期”的常規選舉。
  2. 第二次是在賀錦麗 (Kamala Harris) 辭去副總統後剩下的“短期”的特別選舉。

在賀錦麗當選副總裁後，現任的亞歷杭德羅·帕迪利亞（Alex Padilla）被州長紐森任命他的前參議院席位。 他說他支持全民醫療保險，並共同贊助了綠色新政，但是像南加州的所有其他國會議員一樣，他投票贊成綜合法案，該法案終止了為無保險人民的新冠病毒援助資金，這是基於疫情而獲得的全民醫療的一種形式。

接下來的三個最有資金的候選人是馬克·梅瑟 (Mark Meuser)、科爾迪·威廉姆斯 (Cordie Williams) 和詹姆斯·布拉德利 (James Bradley)。 他們都是共和黨人，每個人都籌集了帕迪拉的一小部分。 他們都不可行。

在短期任期的候選人中，除了帕迪利亞外，丹·奧多德 (Dan O’Dowd) 是針對單一問題的候選人，在“使電腦對人類安全”，及防止汽車以完全自動駕駛模式運行等議題。 在其他短期任期的候選人中，蒂莫西·烏爾西奇 (Timothy Ursich Jr.) 呼籲“重新資助警察”，達芙妮·布拉德福德 (Daphne Bradford) 反對向警察撤資，其餘的都是共和黨人。

Left Unity Slate候選人是約翰·湯普森·帕克 (John Thompson Parker)。 他是社會主義團結黨Socialist Unity Party的成員，也是和平與自由黨Peace and Freedom Party和綠黨Green Party的共同提名人。 他在完整任期選舉的選票上，他也是短任期選舉的可填寫的非原定候選人。

由於加利福尼亞州的前兩名初選中，所有候選人都在11月自動參加決選投票，因此 Left Unity Slate 是一個歷史性的一步，在某些情況下，它可能會利用共和黨候選人之間的分歧將他們排除在決選之外。Knock LA 並不一定同意帕克的所有立場，例如支持烏克蘭的俄羅斯軍事行動。 但是，民選民主黨人缺乏意志承諾並遵循改革的優先事項，這表明帕克與帕迪利亞，和民主黨機構提出了有關國外和國內價值的重要問題的明顯像徵對比，以推薦對他有利的抗議投票。

除了支持撤資在國內警察和海外軍事行動外，帕克還有很長的倡導記錄以阻止美國政府煽動戰爭。 即使只有一名國會議員芭芭拉·李 (Barbara Lee) 投票反對美國對阿富汗的入侵，帕克也對此組織反對。 當時的拜登 (Biden) 迫使參議員投票贊成伊拉克戰爭，帕克組織了反對。 當奧巴馬發動空襲，導致利比亞毀滅和公開奴役非洲人時，帕克倡導反對它。

今天，大多數國會議員都在競相，看誰能在不考慮核武毀滅風險的情況下進行更多升級，投票給帕克傳達了一個信息，我們現在需要的是全民醫療保險和氣候行動，而不是讓世界著火的新保守主義外交政策。

洛杉磯縣

自 2018 年以來，洛杉磯縣陷入了警長亞歷克斯·維拉紐瓦 (Alex Villanueva) 和監事會之間的拉鋸戰。 2020 年，選民批准了法案J，通過將資金從執法部門和監獄中重新分配，來重新構想公共安全。

現在，維拉紐瓦和兩個監事的席位都在選舉中。 其中之一，第 3選區，是一個競爭激烈的開放席位，而維拉紐瓦面臨著眾多強大的挑戰者。 估​稅​員也準備重選。

委員會監​察​員​

​第1選​區: 無建議

第3選​區: 琳賽·霍瓦特 或 亨利·斯特恩 （更新至5/24）

強大的監事會席位在希拉·庫爾 (Sheila Kuehl)之後開放，她是最可靠的改革派 (雖不完美)的投票之一，她決定退休而不是尋求第三個四年制團隊。 這留下了一個關鍵的漏洞，因為監事會正在考慮是否要貫徹最近關於重新構想公共安全的顯著改革舉措。 這些舉措需要資金和政治意願才能充分發揮潛力並真正重塑當地的監獄格局。

如果州參議員鮑勃·赫茨伯格 (Bob Hertzberg) 當選，所有這些改革將會直接逆轉。 赫茨伯格在公共服務方面有著悠久而醜陋的記錄，其中包括在 1990 年代和 2000 年代初期主導了讓聖費爾南多谷從洛杉磯市明顯的種族主義（公平地說，也是階級主義）。他還被指控多次不必要的身體接觸，導致被州參議院小組譴責。

如果那裡有一個破壞性的利益集團，赫茨伯格已經將他們的錢收入囊中，並堅持他們的議程，無論是警察、保釋行業、化石燃料在多個場合、NIMBY 或其他。 他目前還試圖將他缺乏經驗的兒子安插在他原來的州參議院席位上，以確保沒有一絲政治權力從他貪婪的手中溜走。

首要任務是擊敗赫茨伯格。 他的主要對手琳賽·霍瓦特 (Lindsey Horvath)和 亨利·斯特恩 (Henry Stern)中的任何一個都會更好。

現任主管希拉·庫爾 (Sheila Kuehl) 支持西好萊塢市議員琳賽·霍瓦特。 霍瓦特承諾會在強調關顧，和支持超越監禁，她的承諾為她贏得了令人印象深刻的當地改革派背書，包括尤尼斯·埃爾南德斯 (Eunisses Hernández)、La Defensa 和 LA Voice Action。 她反對撤回地方檢察官佐治·賈思森。 她最近還開始與縣警部門抗爭，因為它有向西好萊塢收取服務費用的問題記錄。 重新構想公共安全的領先組織者對霍瓦特作為倡導者充滿信心。

霍瓦特得到了來自各廣泛理念的背書支持，甚至包括議員喬·布斯凱諾 (Joe Buscaino)。 然而，在接受 Ground Game LA 採訪時，霍瓦特對受縣決策影響的環境問題的政策知識似乎很薄弱，這在一個影響如此之多的數百萬人的辦公室中是一個缺點。

州參議員亨利·斯特恩 (Henry Stern) 在環境問題上有著堅定的立場，並且在政策方面和政治方面都對這些問題非常聰明和知識淵博。

他在公共安全方面的記錄喜憂參半。 他投票贊成取消警察資格，並採取強烈的公開立場，支持該縣重塑青年司法系統的努力。 具體來說，斯特恩支持將監獄和監獄的人口歸零，以支持以社區為基礎的關顧，甚至公開反對強大的緩刑官員協會。

但斯特恩最近在 2021 年接受了來自警察工會的競選捐款，他支持紐森的 CARE Court，該法庭會將“低敏銳度”的個人置於限制其權利的非自願監管之下。 對於如何解決洛杉磯縣警部門的持續危機，他一直不置可否。 最近，他呼籲更多的 CHP 官員來處理有組織的零售盜竊等犯罪行為。

在選票上的其他候選人——羅克珊·貝克福德·霍格 (Roxanne Beckford Hoge)、克雷格·A·布里爾(Craig Brill) 和 傑菲·吉爾根蒂 (Jeffi Girgenti)——是極端反動分子和/或沒有開展可行的競選活動。

估​稅​員: 傑弗里·普朗

這個低調的辦公室肩負著評估洛杉磯縣所有應稅房地產和商業財產價值的重要職責。 該辦公室也有腐敗的歷史，前評估員約翰·諾格斯（John Noguez）於 2012 年因收受賄賂以換取降低富人的財產稅估值而被捕。

傑弗里·普朗 (Jeffrey Prang) 是一名持牌評估師，於 2014 年首次當選該辦公室，目前正在競選第三個任期，並且在恢復辦公室誠信方面普遍獲得了積極評價。 Knock LA 稱讚他提高了人們對 19 號提案的意識，如何導致中產階級社區中低收入家庭流離失所的認識。

他的分析類似於 Knock LA 在其 2020 年 11 月的選民指南中，發布的關於19 號提案的內容：雖然重新評估一個人的主要住所以外的財產增加了稅收制度的公平性，對主要住宅進行重新評估的門檻太低，無法阻止多代工人階級家庭，由於財產稅的大幅增加，他們的社區正在迅速仕紳化，因為他們被迫出售房屋。

挑戰者邁克·坎貝爾 (Mike Campbell) 持有反稅收和支持產權的觀點，發誓要保留第 13 號提案，並保護業主免受巨額稅單的影響。 這樣的職位有利於富人，並破壞了為公平的社會服務支付所需的稅收。 其餘的候選人，洛杉磯縣評稅辦公室的僱員桑迪·桑 (Sandy Sun)和安東尼·洛佩茲 (Anthony Lopez)，似乎沒有進行實際的競選活動。 沒有關於他們觀點的信息。

加利福尼亞州州議會

由於加利福尼亞州的前兩名初選中，所有候選人都在11月自動參加決選投票，因此 Left Unity Slate 是一個歷史性的一步，在某些情況下，它可能會利用共和黨候選人之間的分歧將他們排除在決選之外。

Left Unity Slate 得到了和平與自由黨，綠黨和其他尋求左派民主黨替代方案的改革主義者的認可。 當選的民主黨人缺乏執行他們聲稱支持的事情的意願，這使得Left Unity Slate成為我們在全州辦公室的選擇。

州​長: 路易斯·哈維爾·羅德裏格斯

加文·紐森 (Gavin Newsom) 是現任民主黨人。 他從科技公司、低俗的跨國會計師事務所、健康保險公司和能源部門獲得了大量資金。 他聲稱在2018年的競選中要求全民醫療保險，但在美國歷史上最致命的疫情期間，他拒絕推動它。 當大會撥款委員會最終在2022年1月投票贊成單一支付者醫療建議時，紐森聲稱他“沒有看到”該法案。

紐森肯定會晉級並可能在11月贏得大選。 儘管還有其他幾個競爭者（民主黨人，共和黨人，綠黨，NPP），但他們並沒有真正成為紐森的主要威脅。

路易斯·哈維爾·羅德裏格斯 (Luis Javier Rodriguez) 是Left Unity Slate候選人。 他是Tía Chucha的Centro Cultural的創始人，20 多年來一直在聖費爾南多谷東北部 (northeast San Fernando Valley) 提供書店和文化項目，特別關注為處於危險中的青年提供替代方案。 他支持單付款人的醫療保健，以及“結束武裝警員和致命武力”。

副​州​長: 穆罕默德·阿裏夫

現任的康伊蓮 (Eleni Kounalakis) 是民主黨人，並得到前總統奧巴馬、馬世雲 (Fiona Ma)、加利福尼亞民主黨和地方民主黨團體的認可。 她的網頁缺乏問題部分及其當前的“認可”部分。

其他候選人都沒有重要的競選運動或競選財務數據。 康伊蓮 (Kounalakis) 很有機會贏得大選，並且很容易成為初選中的前兩名之一。

穆罕默德·阿裏夫 (Mohammad Arif) 是Left Unity Slate候選人。 他是這場選戰中唯一誓言不採取公司集團捐款的候選人。 他還支持免費的全民醫療保健和教育。 這與副州長的競選直接相關，因為該辦公室的少數實質性職責之一是擔任加利福尼亞大學系統的受託人。

州​務​卿: 加里·N·布倫納

民主黨現任雪麗·N·韋伯 (Shirley Weber)博士在這場競選中籌得最多款項。 她由加文·紐森 (Gavin Newsom) 任命。 以前，她曾是一名立法者，有不同的投票記錄，支持一些警察改革，但也支持特許學校。

加里·N·布倫納 (Gary Blenner) 是 Left Unity Slate候選人。布倫納的平台包括支持排名選擇投票和擴大投票權。

主​計​官: 蘿拉·威爾士

州​平​稅​委​員​會​委​員郭嫻 (Malia Cohen) 是加利福尼亞民主黨的認可候選人。 她擁有比賽中任何民主黨人籌集得最多認可和資金，她很可能會進入決賽。 她的記錄和職位是民主黨候選人的最小問題的，因此，Knock LA是支持Left Unity Slate 候選人蘿拉·威爾士 (Laura Wells)，以便將更保守的候選人拒之門外。 威爾士支持公立住房、公立學校、並為撤資軍方撥款。

在其他候選人中，洛杉磯城市主​計​官羅恩·加爾佩林 (Ron Galperin) 得到了貝蒂·葉 (Betty Yee)的支持，但在種族歧視方面享有聲譽。 州參議員史蒂夫·格雷澤 (Steve Glazer)是立法機關中全民醫療保險的主要反對者之一，並希望禁止運輸工人罷工，而陳仁宜 (Lanhee Chen) 和饒影凡 (Yvonne Yiu) 也為他們的競選活動籌集了大量款項。

財​政​官: 梅根·亞當斯

現任馬世雲 (Fiona Ma) 是民主黨在這場選戰中的領跑者，獲得最多的建制派支持。

安德魯·杜 (Andrew Do) 是共和黨候選人，第二位獲得最多的資金。 奇怪的是，他尚未更新他的社交媒體資料，並且仍在使用2017年的信息。在這場選戰中還有另一個共和黨人和杜一起競選，但他們都沒有任何當前的認可。

梅根·亞當斯 (Meghann Adams) 是她在舊金山公交車司機工會主席，並且參與 Left Unity Slate。 她沒有從公司集團捐助者、房地產開發商、或石油說客那裡拿錢，也是競選中唯一的候選人沒有得到大機構資助。

司​法​部​長: 丹·卡佩洛維茨

民主黨現任羅布·邦塔 (Rob Bonta) 由加文·紐森 (Gavin Newsom) 於2021年任命。保守派之間出現分歧，共和黨人內森·霍克曼 (Nathan Hochman) 、埃裏克·厄利 (Eric Early)和沒有政黨偏好候選人（前共和黨人）安妮·瑪麗·舒伯特 (Anne Marie Schubert) 之間，他們所有人這些都希望能吸引想”嚴厲打擊犯罪”的選民 。 舒伯特是薩克拉門托縣地方檢察官。

Left Unity Slate 候選人丹·卡佩洛維茨（Dan Kapelovitz）是一名刑事辯護律師，並在洛杉磯的一所非營利法學院People’s College of Law教授社會正義倡導者。

州​保​險​局​長: 納塔莉·赫裏齊

現任的裏卡多·拉拉（Ricardo Lara）不僅放棄了不接受他監管的保險公司的競選捐款承諾，而且他的辦公室被抓獲到為一名捐款人辦護，違反了他作為監管機構的角色。

他的主要挑戰者馬克·列文（Marc Levine）並不是特別的改革派。 他反對促進特許學校問責制的法案，還反對允許警長監督委員會的法案。 在這場選舉中，更麻煩的是，在2019年他反對了AB1360，這要求雇主為運輸送貨司機提供保險。 雖然他可能是在決定性競選中問題較小的候選人，但選民可以向他發出信號，以便在大選中向左轉。

Left Unity Slate 候選人納塔莉·赫裏齊（Nathalie Hrizi）呼籲廢除保險公司並以單一付款人制度取而代之。 她是Breaking the Chains的編輯，這是一本女權社會主義雜誌，該雜誌撰寫了大量關於組織拯救墮胎權利的必要性，以及其他主題。

州​平​稅​委​員​會​委​員​，​第 3 選​區: 托尼·巴斯克斯

州​平​稅​委​員​會是一個含糊的國家機構，處理幾個專業的稅收評估領域。 洛杉磯縣托尼·巴斯克斯 (Tony Vazquez) 任職者是前聖塔莫尼卡市長，他是的早期於2019年夏天認可伯尼·桑德斯 (Bernie Sanders) 的人之一。他的兩個挑戰者似乎都沒有在線競選活動或籌集任何競選資金。

其中一個是約翰·門多薩 (John Mendoza) 競選波莫納 (Pomona)的學校董事會，另一個是Y·瑪麗·曼維爾 (Marie Manvel)，為WinRed做出了兩項$1美元的捐款，這是親共和黨相當於 ActBlue。 因為在巴斯克斯任職期間沒有出現任何醜聞，與BOE的過去相比，因此Knock LA 建議投他一票。

公​共​教​育​局​長: 無建議

Dr. Sally Ride Memorial Highway designated as part of the 101 Freeway

Dr. Sally Ride was honored Friday when a portion of the 101 Freeway was named after the trailblazer.

A portion of the freeway will be located between Balboa Avenue and the 405 Freeway and be known as the Dr. Sally Ride Memorial Highway.

"Sally was a transformational figure who captured America's heart, inspired generations of young women and girls to follow their dreams and reach for the stars and ultimately shattered the highest glass ceiling," said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel.

Ride is a beloved American hero and grew up in Encino.

In 1983, Ride became the first American woman in space and also the youngest.

She passed away from cancer in 2012 but left behind a legacy that inspires people of all ages.

California lawmakers urge federal government to take action against gun violence

by: Ashley Zavala

Posted: Jun 3, 2022 / 09:39 AM PDT

Updated: Jun 3, 2022 / 09:39 AM PDT

SACRAMENTO, Calif. (KTXL) — On the eve of National Gun Violence Awareness Day, gun violence prevention groups and a cluster of kids spoke at a rally at the state Capitol Thursday.

“Gun violence is bad for kids because they don’t get to enjoy their lives, they need to be able to enjoy their lives and have a long happy life,” one kid said at the rally.

State lawmakers are urging Congress and the federal government to take action after a series of horrific shootings across the state and nation.

“We’re here year after year, shooting after shooting, and nothing gets done,” said State Sen. Susan Rubio (D-Baldwin Park).

Democratic lawmakers vowed to fast-track a new set of gun control bills to add to the more than 100 existing laws in California.

“We’re going to expedite a number of bills and have several new laws in this state by the end of this month,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Woodland Hills).

Just before Thursday’s rally, lawmakers in the assembly from both sides of the aisle unanimously agreed on House Resolution 107 relating to National Gun Violence Awareness Day, acknowledging they can work together to stop shootings.

“We have to bring both of these together, if we’re going to have bills, let’s have consequences,” said Assemblymember Laura Davis (R-Laguna Niguel).

“We can pass all the laws that we want to pass but criminals do not follow laws, so if we want to be honest about fighting gun violence, and passing common-sense gun laws that I support, we need to go after criminals,” said Assemblymember Al Muratsuchi (D-Torrance).

But toward the end of what was a unified discussion, Democratic Assemblyman Adrian Nazarin took aim at Republicans.

“If we want to make action happen, we don’t just get up and spew garbage, because lives have been lost,” Nazarin said. “Stop this garbage here, “we can work together”, I’m done.”

Facing new law, plastics lobby turns to mailers; Industry sends fliers falsely claiming that consumers will bear cost of tighter rules.

By Susanne Rust

Cheryl Auger was stunned this month when one of her Pasadena neighbors and friends received a flier in the mail featuring her state assemblyman, with a line stating, "Higher taxes on plastic products will enrich corporate interests with no guarantee of reducing plastic waste."

Although she didn't know it at the time, Auger's friend was on the receiving end of a plastics industry campaign to pressure state lawmakers into weakening proposed restrictions on single-use containers, which legislators are mulling in bill form and which could become a November ballot measure.

"What is surprising to me is a lack of culpability," said Auger, a plastic waste activist.

The mailers, sent by a group calling itself the Environmental Solutions Coalition, assert without attribution that bans on single-use plastics "will have a devastating impact on working families" by driving up costs for consumers. Unmentioned in the mailings are that plastics manufacturers and other industries are financing the coalition.

The fliers are all aimed at Democrats, largely in Southern California, possibly in an attempt to pressure them into derailing the November ballot measure by enacting watered-down legislation the industry can accept.

"I interpret it as a message, as a warning to members of the Legislature," said Assembly Member Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), whose constituents received one of the mailers. "If that's the intent, it's backfired because it's made us even more committed to trying to pass meaningful legislation to crack down on plastic pollution."

In the current legislative session, lawmakers are working on a bill designed to reduce plastic waste. If they are unable to draft legislation by June 30, the issue will go straight to voters as a ballot measure.

The initiative, the California Recycling and Plastic Pollution Reduction Act, would require all single-use plastic packaging and food ware used in California to be recyclable, reusable, refillable or compostable by 2030. Single-use plastic production would have to be reduced by 25% by 2030. The costs of the program are to be borne by the producers and distributors of single-use plastics, and the language explicitly states the costs cannot be passed on to the consumer.

U.S. industries for decades have formed seeming "grass-roots groups" to push agendas such as lower taxes and fewer restrictions on tobacco and pollution. The groups behind the Environmental Solutions Coalition include the California Business Roundtable and the American Chemistry Council, which includes plastics manufacturers and oil companies.

Members of the coalition have stated they'd prefer to see the issue settled in the Legislature.

The coalition's mailers targeted constituents of at least five lawmakers -- Assembly Members Gabriel, Chris Holden (DPasadena), Eduardo Garcia (D-Coachella), Jacqui Irwin (D-Thousand Oaks) and Rebecca Bauer-Kahan (D-Orinda). None were consulted before their images were included in the mailers, according to Michael Bustamante, a spokesman for the coalition.

Holden could not be reached for comment, and Garcia's office said it was unaware of the fliers.

Irwin sent a statement saying she preferred a legislative solution to the problem of plastic waste, and as yet has not "taken a position on the single use plastics initiative."

Bauer-Kahan said she had never heard of the Environmental Solutions Coalition, "nor have I had any conversations with them regarding any initiative." She said she supported a reduction of single-use plastics and she has consistently supported legislation to "curb plastic pollution."

Like his colleagues, Gabriel said he wants the Legislature to solve the issue, but described the mailers and intimidation campaign as "unsettling" and "confusing."

"As a pure matter of politics, I think it's a very poorly done piece," he said about the flier's messaging. "I don't know anyone who can figure out exactly what it's trying to communicate."

In California and some other states, plastics restrictions are gaining momentum because of evolving research into their health and environmental impacts.

Plastics never fully degrade. They just break down into smaller and smaller pieces called microplastics. These particles often contain harmful chemical additives such as flame retardants or plasticizers. Reports suggest that humans consume roughly a credit card's worth of microplastic each week.

Over the last year, research has shown the presence of these particles in human blood, healthy lung tissue and meconium -the first bowel movement of a newborn. They are also found in marine organisms, ocean water, air and soil. Some researchers project that by 2050, there may be more plastic by weight in the world's oceans than there are fish.

Nick Lapis, director of advocacy for Californians Against Waste, said he found it revealing that the plastics industry decided to hide behind layers of trade associations and front groups, instead of making its pitch directly to voters.

"This kind of deceptive action is exactly the issue that the attorney general raised a couple weeks ago," said Lapis, whose nonprofit group has advocated on waste and recycling issues since 1977.

Last month, California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta, announced a first-of-its-kind investigation into the fossil fuel and petrochemical industries for their alleged role in causing and exacerbating a global crisis in plastic waste pollution. Bonta accused them of "perpetuating a myth that recycling can solve the plastics crisis."

Bustamante, the spokesman for the Environmental Solutions Coalition, also was unable to succinctly sum up the message of the fliers, but said they targeted legislators in the Los Angeles area who he considered "part of a common-sense coalition."

He said the mailer was sent to the constituents of lawmakers who "have historically been on the record as paying very close attention to the kinds of things and issues that could increase costs to their constituents."

The fliers do not explicitly mention the pending legislation or the initiative, but stated that "adding billions of dollars in higher costs on the backs of working families is the wrong way to do it."

Auger, a cybersecurity specialist who co-founded a refill store in Pasadena to help consumers reduce plastic waste, said she was not completely surprised by the front group's scare tactics. The industry, she said, has "stymied anything significant on plastics since the 1990s."

Caption: PHOTO: THE FLIER targeting Democrats seems to be aimed at weakening a bill restricting single-use containers.

Aliso CanyonEnvironmentVoter GuideElections

Knock LA asked several state and county candidates for their position on transitioning LA away from oil and gas.

Patty Crost Glueck

|

May 21, 2022

FacebookTweetPinLinkedIn

Los Angeles residents will vote in crucial local elections on June 7, 2022, yet many candidates have failed to to take positions on key environmental positions. Without clean air and water, our planet is not livable, and when climate change is out of control, so are storms and wildfires.

Knock LA therefore asked candidates in five contested state and county races in the San Fernando Valley and Westside for their stances on four crucial environmental topics: banning gas hookups in new buildings; subsidies for climate-friendly building appliances; closing the Aliso Canyon and Playa del Rey gas storage sites; and requiring 2,500-foot setbacks from oil and gas facilities.

The combustion of gas, often used to heat homes or power cooking stoves, emits a significant amount of planet-warming gases like methane and carbon dioxide, in addition to other pollutants associated with negative respiratory health effects. Alternatives such as electric heat pumps and induction stoves remove the need for gas, operating instead on an electric grid increasingly powered by renewable energy.

While over 50 California cities and counties have now banned gas hookups in new buildings, statewide action has lagged. Efforts to pass setbacks between oil and gas facilities and vulnerable communities failed to pass the state legislature in 2021 due to state Senator Bob Hertzberg and other senators. A measure to close the Aliso Canyon gas storage facilities is currently being considered in the state Legislature. Read about local candidates’ positions on these key issues below.

Supervisorial District 3 (includes SFV, West LA to West Hollywood):

1. Are you in favor of a ban on gas hookups in new buildings?

Lindsey Horvath: Yes.

Henry Stern: Yes.

Bob Hertzberg: [No response]

Craig Brill: No.

2. Are you in favor of subsidies given to individuals and companies to replace gas appliances with fuel pumps, induction stoves, and other appliances that do not use methane?

Lindsey Horvath: Yes

Henry Stern: Yes

Bob Hertzberg: [No response]

Craig Brill: No, natural gas is the cleanest fossil fuel that has allowed us to reduce our carbon emissions. Our reliance on solar and wind do not produce enough energy, so we are now relying on imported power from dirty diesel. We must move to new nuclear technology. It is the only 100% carbon-free stable and cheap energy. Energy like water is life.

3. Are you in favor of closing gas storage facilities such as the Aliso Canyon and Playa del Rey gas storage sites (and using pipelines from out-of-state sources until they’re no longer needed)?

Lindsey Horvath: Yes.

Henry Stern: Yes.

Bob Hertzberg: [No response]

Craig Brill: I favor closure of Aliso Canyon — it should be relocated away from residential areas and groundwater storage. I do not support importing through pipelines from other states or countries. This will raise costs for Californians and disproportionately hurt the poor and middle class.

4. Are you in favor of 2,500-foot setbacks between oil and gas facilities (production, storage) and communities (homes, schools, parks)?

Lindsey Horvath: Yes

Henry Stern: Yes

Bob Hertzberg: [No response]

Craig Brill: Yes

Other candidates for this office not responding: Jeffi Girgenti, Roxanne Hoge

Candidates for State Senate SD 20 (includes Van Nuys, Granada Hills, Sylmar, Tujunga, Reseda):

1. Are you in favor of a ban on gas hookups in new buildings?

Caroline Menjivar: Yes, I believe all our new commercial and residential buildings should be created in a sustainable way with clean energy.

Daniel Hertzberg: [No response]

Seydi Alejandra Morales: Yes. I am in favor of utilizing our new technology, including renewable energy technology, to create more sustainable housing within our communities. We now have technology that can achieve the same output we get now that is significantly more efficient but does not harm the environment. Additionally, in implementing these new technologies ensuring the creation and/or transition of jobs within the renewable energy space.

2. Are you in favor of subsidies given to individuals and companies to replace gas appliances with fuel pumps, induction stoves, and other appliances that do not use methane?

Caroline Menjivar: Yes. We should also be retrofitting our buildings with equipment that is clean-energy. Old, broken Air conditioners should be replaced with heat pumps. Property owners of multi-family dwellings should be given incentives and subsidies for bringing solar to their buildings and transferring savings to tenants’ utility bills. We should be focusing on incentivizing individuals who are doing their part to remove ourselves from a fossil fuel dependency. We can’t simply focus on the supply portion of fossil fuels, but also [must] talk about decreasing the demand side of the story.

Daniel Hertzberg: [No response]

Seydi Alejandra Morales: Yes. Utilizing subsidies to help our communities become more sustainable is a good use of California’s surplus funds. Allowing for these subsidies will decrease toxic materials … emitting into our environment, which in turn will have longer-lasting positive effects [on] our health and environment. More importantly, I would support and push for policy that replaces gas appliances, but this must also be done in conjunction with other sustainable sources of production that will power those appliances with sustainable renewable energy that is affordable for all members of the communities.

3. Are you in favor of closing gas storage facilities such as the Aliso Canyon and Playa del Rey gas storage sites (and using pipelines from out-of-state sources until they’re no longer needed)?

Caroline Menjivar: Yes. I am excited to see Senator Stern’s bill calling for the [shutdown] of Aliso Canyon, a facility that is directly impacting the community I am looking to represent.

Daniel Hertzberg: [No response]

Seydi Alejandra Morales: Yes. I believe attention must be given, especially to frontline communities in identifying immediate need for environmental equity and health access provision. Particularly as it relates to the contamination in the ambient air and water table.

4. Are you in favor of 2,500-foot setbacks between oil and gas facilities (production, storage) and communities (homes, schools, parks)?

Caroline Menjivar: Yes, at minimum, this is what we need to do, until we end our dependency on fossil fuels.

Daniel Hertzberg: [No response]

Seydi Alejandra Morales: Yes. If oil and gas facilities are necessary, I am in support of placing these facilities in areas that are … a safe distance from communities, where they will not immediately and directly impact people within close proximity of these facilities. Further, I support the creation of a holistic manner of building and/or structuring an organic plan to begin remediation practices and changes that will clean up contaminated lands in order to be able to use that land in some other, more useful manner that better serves the communities.

Other candidates for this office not responding are: Ely De La Cruz Ayao

Candidates for Assembly AD 40 (including Santa Clarita, Chatsworth, Porter Ranch, Northridge, Granada Hills):

None of the candidates for this office responded (Pilar Schiavo, Suzette Martinez Valladares, Annie E. Cho)

Candidates for Assembly AD 44 (includes Glendale, Tujunga, Shadow Hills):

1. Are you in favor of a ban on gas hookups in new buildings?

Laura Friedman: Yes. My bill AB3232 is one of the key measures that has begun this process in California.

Barry Jacobsen: No.

2. Are you in favor of subsidies given to individuals and companies to replace gas appliances with fuel pumps, induction stoves, and other appliances that do not use methane?

Laura Friedman: Yes. I recently installed an induction stove at home and absolutely love it!

Barry Jacobsen: No.

3. Are you in favor of closing gas storage facilities such as the Aliso Canyon and Playa del Rey gas storage sites (and usingpipelines from out-of-state sources until they’re no longer needed)?

Laura Friedman: Yes and no. I have been a vocal opponent of the Aliso Canyon facility, however, as we work to eliminate the use of fossil fuels in California, we need to evaluate the entire environmental impacts of where we get our gas so that we are choosing the least environmentally damaging option. If closing a specific site forces us to use pipelines that actually generate more net carbon emissions, or leave negative impacts on disadvantaged communities, then we would need to consider those factors prior to making that decision. We should always look where we are doing the least harm.

Barry Jacobsen: No.

4. Are you in favor of 2,500-foot setbacks between oil and gas facilities (production, storage) and communities (homes, schools, parks)?

Laura Friedman: Yes.

Barry Jacobsen: [I] would need to look further into this suggestion, including the cost implications to the companies and tax payers (if any).

Candidates for Assembly AD 46 (Includes Van Nuys, Granada Hills, Reseda):

None of the candidates for this office responded (Dana Caruso and Jesse Gabriel)

Candidates for Assembly AD 51 (includes West LA, Beverly Hills, Santa Monica, West Hollywood):

1. Are you in favor of a ban on gas hookups in new buildings?

Louis Abramson: Yes.

Rick Chavez Zbur: [No response]

2. Are you in favor of subsidies given to individuals and companies to replace gas appliances with fuel pumps, induction stoves, and other appliances that do not use methane?

Louis Abramson: Yes.

Rick Chavez Zbur: [No response]

3. Are you in favor of closing gas storage facilities such as the Aliso Canyon and Playa del Rey gas storage sites (and using pipelines from out-of-state sources until they’re no longer needed)?

Louis Abramson: Yes.

Rick Chavez Zbur: [No response]

4. Are you in favor of 2,500-foot setbacks between oil and gas facilities (production, storage) and communities (homes, schools, parks)?

Louis Abramson: Yes — I also support Gov. Newsom’s proposal to extend that to 3200 feet.

Rick Chavez Zbur: [No response]

Matt Haney’s Jewish roots: public service, social justice and doing his grandpa proud

Emma Goss

Upon taking the oath of office at his swearing-in ceremony for the state Assembly on May 4, San Francisco’s Matt Haney also became the 19th member of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus.

On Thursday, he will be part of a caucus meeting with Gov. Gavin Newsom, marking Haney’s first audience with the governor — San Francisco’s former mayor — since joining the Assembly. Among the topics on the table is how much funding Newsom’s proposed budget will be allocating for Holocaust education in the fiscal year that begins July 1.

“That’s something that’s been important to me,” Haney, 40, told J. over Zoom from his Sacramento office, noting that his first job after graduating from UC Berkeley was working as a docent at the Museum of Tolerance in Los Angeles. He also worked on Holocaust education programming when serving on the San Francisco Board of Education from 2012 to 2019, part of it as president.

You won’t find any mention of Haney’s Jewish roots on his Wikipedia page, and aside from publicly lighting the Hanukkah menorah in Union Square in 2020 alongside Chabad Rabbi Yosef Langer, Haney’s Jewish identity has flown under the radar throughout his career in politics.

But you will find his 94-year-old Jewish grandfather, Allen Calvin, prominent on Haney’s Instagram.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Matt Haney (@matthaneysf)

“Grateful for their love and support, and the inspiration they’ve give[n] me to serve others” Haney captioned a May 13 post that included a picture of Grandpa Allen and Grandma Dorothy, also 94, along with his cousins, who were at the Golden State Warriors’ winning playoff game against the Memphis Grizzlies.

“A lot of my Jewish identity was also formed through my relationship with my grandfather,” Haney told J.

Grandpa Allen grew up in St. Paul, Minnesota, the son of Jewish immigrant parents from Eastern Europe. His family faced antisemitism as one of only a few Jewish families in their neighborhood. Allen joined the Navy at 17, fought in World War II and later developed a close relationship with Martin Luther King Jr. and Coretta Scott King, devoting his life to education and civil rights.

Haney said his grandfather instilled a strong commitment to Jewish values that connect to the “experience of persecution and discrimination,” which in turn brought him to develop his own “understanding of responsibility around it.”

That history, Haney said, shaped “our whole family’s understanding of our Jewish identity and…a broader commitment of service and our responsibility to others.”

Family Hanukkah and Passover celebrations took place at his grandparents’ home in Golden Gate Heights, where they still live. They’re also longtime members of Congregation Emanu-El.

Haney’s parents divorced when he was 4. He and his sister, Erin Haney, 41, were brought up in the East Bay by their mother, whose work focused on children’s health advocacy and policy. Now retired, she’s an author of murder-mystery novels set in Sacramento. A third sibling, Nathan Calvin, 25, was born when Matt was 15.

Raised in a secular home, Haney didn’t grow up attending synagogue or have a bar mitzvah, though the family traveled to Israel multiple times to see cousins who live there. After college, he went back to Israel on a Taglit Birthright trip.

He developed a stronger connection to Judaism as he got older. While leading tours at the Museum of Tolerance for a short time after graduating from Cal, Haney said he “started to connect more to my Jewish identity and the responsibility as a Jew of really protecting minority rights and human rights.”

He took that to heart and put it into action. Haney spent his early 20s in Bosnia working in the Special Department for War Crimes in the Prosecutor’s Office of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He then went to the National University of Ireland where he got a master’s degree in human rights. He also picked up a couple of degrees at Stanford, a master’s in education and his law degree.

Haney handily won the April 19 special election to replace David Chiu (who resigned after being named San Francisco city attorney) after serving since 2019 on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors. He represented District 6, which includes the Tenderloin, the neighborhood where he’s lived for eight years.

Haney is fiercely devoted to the immigrant-rich Tenderloin community, which mirrors his connection to Judaism and its history of persecution.

“The Tenderloin is a place where we really challenge ourselves to live our values of compassion and healing,” Haney said. “The people who were hurt or harmed are a reflection of trauma that happened elsewhere, overwhelmingly, and they’re in the Tenderloin because they’re trying to get some help there. So there’s actually a lot that’s really powerful and beautiful about a neighborhood that is really a beacon of compassion.”

Haney lives in a rent-controlled apartment (which he considers a luxury) with his two orange tabby cats. He is one of only three elected officials in the 120-member state Legislature who are publicly known to be renters rather than homeowners.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Matt Haney (@matthaneysf)

“[That’s] pretty incredible, considering about half of the state are renters, but only less than 2 percent of the state Legislature,” Haney said. Many renters live with few protections, he said, and as a result are in a constant state of instability and uncertainty.

“The rent can go up and they can be forced to move from their home,” Haney said. He understands the anxiety that comes with displacement — he moved with his family to 15 different East Bay locations before he turned 18, due to rent increases or because the place they were renting was being sold. “I think it’s important for policymakers to understand.”

Haney said the issues in the Tenderloin that he worked on as San Francisco supervisor — homelessness, drug addiction, access to health care — are what motivated him to run for state office.

“I don’t think that the problems that we see in the Tenderloin can be solved in the Tenderloin,” Haney said. While the problems of inequity are highly concentrated in his neighborhood, he said, they’re also ubiquitous across the Bay Area.

As he grows into his new role in the state Assembly, Haney said he is honored to serve on the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, which advocates on behalf of the professional, educational, social, political and cultural concerns of the Jewish Community. He and the caucus chair, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (San Fernando Valley), graduated in the same class at UC Berkeley.

Haney brings an “extraordinary record of standing up for vulnerable communities,” Gabriel said in a phone interview with J., which he said is in keeping with the value of tikkun olam (repairing the world) that is also part of the caucus’ mission. 

“We think he’s going to be a huge asset, and be a major player in the Legislature on uplifting the most vulnerable folks in California, irrespective of their background,” Gabriel added.

Haney said being new to Sacramento, he’s found a supportive community through the caucus.

“It’s just amazing to see the work that the Jewish legislators are doing on such a wide variety of issues that I know have been driven in part by their Jewish values,” Haney said.

Now he’s one of them.

Hundreds descend on Sacramento to lobby for Jewish interests

Gabe Stutman

Willie Armstrong, the chief of staff to state Assemblymember Chris Holden, looked rushed. The former Air Force service member, wearing a dark suit and an American flag pinned to his lapel, had only 10 or 15 minutes to spare before he needed to get back to his office during a busy period in the legislative calendar.

With his fingers clasped in front of him, Armstrong nevertheless listened politely as a half-dozen Jewish lobbyists — unpaid ones, gathered in the common area of a Sacramento office building — began to nudge Armstrong to nudge his boss, the powerful chair of the Assembly’s Appropriations Committee, to support seven Jewish priority legislative measures.

Armstrong made eye contact and asked questions, particularly about surveying the state of Holocaust education. Holden, of Pasadena, already supported some of the measures being discussed; others Armstrong said he would look into. The chief of staff remained standing throughout the brief meeting.

It was a scene replicated in dozens of lawmakers’ offices last week, when the most influential Jewish advocacy network in California state politics — the Jewish Public Affairs Committee, or JPAC — held its annual keynote convention, in person, for the first time in three years.

Over two days, hundreds of politically minded Jews convened and then reconvened for speeches, award ceremonies and policy discussions in the seventh-floor ballroom of Sacramento’s elegant Citizen Hotel. The event drew big names in California politics — Attorney General Rob Bonta and Lt. Gov. Eleni Kounalakis among them — and in the worlds of Jewish philanthropy, lawmaking and business. There was a lot of schmoozing and networking. The lines for food were long.

The culmination of the policy conference, though, is “Advocacy Day,” which happens on the second day. JPAC describes it as an “advocacy experience” — sort of like a Major League Baseball fantasy camp for the politically minded.

JPAC was established 50 years ago with the goal of uniting Jewish community interests under one umbrella group in the state capital. In 2020 it canceled its conference because of the pandemic, and last year the event was held virtually.

The organization defines itself in many ways — as “the voice of California’s Jewish community”; as the “largest single-state coalition” of Jewish community organizations in the country; as “California’s organized Jewish community convener.”

What it really is is an advocacy (or lobbying) organization that purports to represent California’s approximately 1.2 million Jews. A daunting task, considering the range of political opinions held by Jewish Californians. Nevertheless, with some nimble political maneuvering, JPAC aims to build consensus around a slate of bills each year.

“We recognize the value of coming together under one voice,” executive director David Bocarsly said in a recent interview. “It allows us to all gain.”

Bocarsly, 31, a Conservative Jew who wears a kippah, was hired away from the California Legislative Jewish Caucus late last year. He now quarterbacks the whole thing along with the JPAC board and with help from Cliff Berg, a registered lobbyist in Sacramento.

To form its agenda, JPAC works with 30 partner organizations (Federations, Jewish Community Relations Councils, the Anti-Defamation League and other nonprofits), whose leaders sit on the JPAC board.

Some of the bills it chooses to back affect the Jewish community directly — such as funding for the Nonprofit Security Grant Program, which bolsters synagogue security, or state funds to support Holocaust centers in San Francisco and L.A. Others are not so direct — funding for food benefits for undocumented immigrants and a slate of bills that tackle poverty and health care.

JPAC has also advocated for gun control measures, affordable housing and bills that combat human trafficking.

“I like to say the work falls under two pillars, the first being support for core Jewish community needs. And the second being support for core Jewish community values,”  Bocarsly said.

“And we’re careful not to touch on issues that might be too polarizing to some of our community organizations,” he added.

This year JPAC selected 38 bills and budget priorities to support. The full list can be viewed here.

A 501(c)4 nonpartisan nonprofit, JPAC raises money primarily through membership dues paid by its partner organizations. It also charges between $100 and $150 for tickets to Advocacy Day (plus add-ons for special VIP opportunities, such as dinner with the California Legislative Jewish Caucus). Bocarsly said the fees help fund the event but don’t fully cover its costs.

The convention saw Bonta and Kounalakis give keynote addresses on the importance of combating antisemitism, and lawmaker-led panels including “combating hate through coalition-building” and “serving immigrants, refugees, and asylum-seekers.”

The conference this year saw about 200 attendees, many of them affiliated with JPAC partner organizations like Jewish Family and Children’s Services and Jewish Federations, and others not affiliated directly with large nonprofits. The ADL brought one of the event’s largest contingents.

On Advocacy Day, JPAC splits all of the attendees into groups of about a half-dozen people. Each group is given a list of legislative priorities (this year it was five bills and two budget requests) that are among JPAC’s top asks. After a brief prep session, the groups fan out to the surrounding Capitol office buildings to take meetings with lawmakers and their staff.

JPAC provides instructions, spelling out the dos and don’ts of political lobbying: Do “be brief and to the point.” Do “read the legislator’s body language.” Do not “belabor your concerns,” and do not “mention fundraising or money.”

The goal is to talk to as many legislative offices as possible. This year, JPAC advocacy groups spoke with 88 of the 120 total.

J. tagged along with one of the advocacy groups, an effort that began with a strategy session over coffee and tea in the ballroom. Our group, or “team,” ranged in age, religious observance and experience with political advocacy.

Each person picked an issue from JPAC’s list they would take the lead on. Renee, a man with a closely cropped gray beard and cloth cap, had parents who survived the Holocaust and many relatives who did not. He picked a Senate bill targeting Holocaust education. Eli, a slight, retired physician who wore a matching pin and tie depicting the Israeli and American flags flying together, would advocate for measures to increase food and health benefits for undocumented immigrants.

Josh, a Chinese-born, millennial Jew and the only kippah-wearing member of the group, would vouch for an increase in Nonprofit Security Grant Funding. Fellow millennial Jeff, a public policy professional with JFCS in San Francisco, would talk about the hate symbols bill introduced by East Bay Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan. Cathy, team leader and coach wearing a polka dot blouse, made sure everyone was on the same page and spoke across a number of different topics. Donna, the wife of the retired physician, said she preferred not to speak during the meetings but offered her two cents every now and then.

After a fajita lunch, we walked a few blocks to a temporary legislative office building (the Capitol complex is under construction). The building was thronged with activity, not only JPAC advocates but others, including medical industry lobbyists wearing white coats.

Our first stop was at Holden’s office where we met with the chief of staff.

We had seven topics to hit and only minutes for each because of Armstrong’s time constraints. After some hurried introductions and the exchange of business cards, Renee spoke about SB 693, which would create a large-scale study to assess Holocaust and genocide education in California. He told of his parents’ escape from Nazi-occupied Europe to Shanghai. He said many of their relatives were murdered, and referenced research showing about two-thirds of millennials don’t know basic facts about the Holocaust, including that 6 million Jews were killed.

Armstrong’s demeanor began to soften. He couldn’t hear Renee well, so he moved closer, to the other side of the table where he’d been standing.

“If we do not learn from history, it will repeat,” Josh offered.

Armstrong listened attentively to Renee and to the rest of the presentations. He asked questions about funding, and where each bill was in the legislative process.

After 10 minutes or so, he told us his time was up, and he hustled back to his office.

The next stop was with, notably, a Republican lawmaker — the only one on our list. But since JPAC is a nonpartisan organization, nobody in our group used the word “Republican.” Instead we said the representative was with the “minority party.”

Thurston “Smitty” Smith is a former construction worker and cement company owner representing a vast district in southeastern California. Much of his district consists of the Mojave Desert, and its economy is powered by military bases.

“I’m just a guy who worked construction,” Smith joked.

He invited all of us into his small office. We wheeled in chairs, while Smith sat behind his desk next to a legislative aide.

On the wall was an American flag with the “DONT TREAD ON ME” symbol. Eli admired the flag and said he considered buying a similar one after 9/11.

Smith seemed to fully back some of our group’s bills. “I think we should have a whole semester on World War II history,” he said in support of the Holocaust education bill.

On some of the other bills, he was receptive but noncommittal.

The group asked Smith to support the budget measures to add food and health benefits for undocumented immigrants, and for seniors.

“I don’t see who benefits from people going hungry,” Eli said. “Particularly in the construction business. I don’t think you want someone who’s hungry fixing a roof.”

“What’s the request? Billions? Millions?” Smith said, adding that he does food deliveries for seniors as a volunteer.

He said if it were mere millions he could probably support it. But he also expressed reservations about the size of Gov. Gavin Newsom’s anticipated budget proposal. He said his staff had placed bets about how many tens of billions of dollars the Democrat would propose in spending.

Smith cracked jokes and showed the group some of the knickknacks in his office, like a trophy from coaching Little League baseball. He said he was one of the few lawmakers in Sacramento who owned a business, experience the group seemed to agree was sorely needed in the statehouse. He enthusiastically agreed to a group photo.

Our next stop was with a friend of JPAC — Assemblymember Marc Berman of Palo Alto, a member of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus. Berman hosted us in a conference room alongside a young staffer.

“I don’t think we need to do much lobbying with you!” Jeff said to laughter.

We had a free-flowing conversation not only about JPAC’s budget priorities, but about Berman’s other legislative priorities.

Jeff, the millennial public policy director with JFCS, asked Berman which among JPAC’s bills he anticipated would see the strongest opposition. Berman said AB 587, introduced by Jesse Gabriel, the Jewish caucus chair. The measure would require social media companies to report to Sacramento on policies moderating hate speech, and on efforts to combat hate online. Groups like the ADL continue to advocate for more regulation of hate speech on the internet, including with this bill.

“I’m sure tech folks are opposed to it, and will be working hard against it,” Berman said, noting the bill would add a regulatory hurdle for social media companies, including those in his Silicon Valley district.

The conversation was casual; it was clear Berman already supported JPAC’s priorities. Describing his priorities for the year outside of JPAC bills, he named workforce development, particularly in the health care space, and programs to train teachers to teach computer science.

Our last stop was with San Francisco’s newly elected Assemblymember, Matt Haney. Haney wasn’t available, so we met with staffer Nate Allbee.

Haney had been sworn in only a week prior. It seemed the office was still being set up — Allbee didn’t even have his official email address yet.

We presented our bills. Josh talked about increasing funding to $80 million for the security grant program. He said funding was needed not only for physical features like gates and security doors, but for person-to-person trainings on how to de-escalate situations before they become violent.

RELATED: Matt Haney’s Jewish roots — public service, social justice and doing his grandpa proud

Churches don’t need security. But synagogues do, Josh pointed out.

Allbee listened politely. Asked about Haney’s priorities, Allbee said confronting the fentanyl epidemic in San Francisco was at the top of the list. Eli, the physician, recommended an expert on the subject of addiction and withdrawal, and Allbee seemed to appreciate the referral.

Outside Haney’s office, team leader Cathy seemed pleased with everyone’s efforts. It was time to head back to the Bay Area, where most of us lived. We exchanged contact information and left.

To JPAC, the day appeared to be a major success. It was Bocarsly’s first year organizing the event. He called the convention “amongst the largest JPAC Advocacy Days in its history.”

“We had the most legislators participate in our conference than ever before, and we had the most meetings with legislative offices than ever before.”

Days after Advocacy Day, the governor released his revised May budget draft. JPAC sent an email to all of the attendees soon after.

“I’m blown away,” wrote Bocarsly. “As a result of our lobbying efforts, Governor Newsom included $93.2 million for JPAC priority items into his state budget proposal.”

JPAC didn’t get everything it wanted — Newsom’s budget included $50 million for the NPSG, not $80 million. But “The #CAJewishVoice is being heard,” Bocarsly wrote, adding an emoji of an arm, flexing its muscle.

Bill will address illegal street racing - Beverly Press & Park Labrea News

May 19, 2022

Bill will address illegal street racing

The California State Assembly on May 16 passed Assembly Bill 2000, which aims to prevent street racing and vehicle sideshows from occurring in parking lots.

The measure, authored by Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel (D-Woodland Hills), expands options for law enforcement to crack down on dangerous driving.

“Far too frequently, street racing and illegal sideshows devastate families, harm innocent bystanders and cut short young lives,” Gabriel said. “Communities across California are sick and tired of this reckless behavior. This bipartisan legislation will crack down on dangerous activity and help to save lives.”

An increase in illegal street racing activity occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic, the assemblyman said. In 2020, the California Highway Patrol responded to more than 25,000 calls involving illegal street racing activity statewide, an alarming increase of more than 3,500 calls from the year before, he added.

Law enforcement officials are using driver’s license suspensions as a tool to deter illegal street racing. AB 2000 will allow courts to suspend a driver’s license upon conviction for exhibition of speed during a sideshow in a parking lot – an area not currently covered under law. AB 2000 will next be considered by the California Senate, where it is expected to be heard in a policy committee in the coming weeks.

Bill That Expands Scope of Illegal Street Racing Passes Assembly – California Globe

AB 2000 would expand street racing to include parking lots

By Evan Symon, May 17, 2022 4:16 pm

A bill that would expand the scope of the ban on illegal street races in California passed the Assembly on Monday.

Assembly Bill 2000, authored by Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel (D-Woodland Hills), would crack down further on illegal street racing, as well as similar “sideshows” and other non-legal events. Specifically, illegal street racing would be expanded beyond highways and streets. Under AB 2000, they would also now be illegal to do in off street parking lots.

Assemblyman Gabriel wrote the bill to combat the rise in street racing in the last few years. During the COVID-19 pandemic, especially in the early days, empty streets enticed many street racers. This led to not only a major surge in California and across the country, but also many resultant deaths. In a statement, Gabriel noted that three people were killed during an illegal street race in Burbank in August 2021, a Woodland Hills woman was killed during a race in October 2021, and the arrest of over three dozen people at several illegal street racing gatherings in Los Angeles.

AB 2000 would also serve as an expansion to last years passed bill AB 3, which increased the penalties for illegally street racing.

 “Far too frequently, street racing and illegal sideshows devastate families, harm innocent bystanders, and cut short young lives,” Assemblyman Gabriel said. “Communities in the San Fernando Valley and across California are sick and tired of this reckless behavior. This bipartisan legislation will crack down on dangerous activity and help to save lives.”

Bipartisan support for AB 2000

 Since being introduced in February, AB 2000 has received widespread support from both Democrats and Republicans. Including the Assembly vote on Monday, all votes to date have been unanimous. The message of preventing deaths has swayed any opposition to the bill, with no lawmaker or group currently being on record in opposition. Testimony from those who have lost loved ones due to illegal street races in particular has been a compelling influencer for many.

 “AB 2000 will help us save lives, and prevent further crashes and drivers going to prison for manslaughter,” said Lili Trujillo, Founder and Executive Director of Street Racing Kills, a non-profit created in 2014 after Trujillo’s 16-year-old daughter, Valentina, was killed in a street racing incident. “An exhibition of speed in a parking lot is way too common now and people are being hurt and killed, AB 2000 is definitely a great tool to help us save lives.”

 Assemblyman Vince Fong (R-Bakersfield) also added on Tuesday that “There are countless stories every week throughout California about illegal street races and dangerous sideshows shutting down streets, causing accidents, damaging neighborhoods, and endangering lives. They are unpredictable, destructive, and can lead to senseless deaths that devastate families. AB 2000 is an important and needed step in cracking down on illegal sideshows to make our communities safer and save lives.”

Capitol insiders told the Globe on Tuesday that AB 2000 would likely pass in the coming months.

“This is one of those bills that is only voted against on accident,” explained “Dana,” a State Capitol staffer, to the Globe. “It would be very surprising  if this bill is seriously challenged in the Senate or by Governor Newsom. To many this is a common sense measure and to others this is a law that will reduce street racing and will result in the arrest of more for having done it. Something to like in it for everyone.”

AB 2000 is due to be heard in Senate committees in the coming weeks.

Elections 2022: Legislator Jesse Gabriel faces newcomer Dana Caruso in Assembly District 46

Gillian Moran, Contributing Writer

In the June 7 primary contest for the open 46th Assembly District seat, San Fernando Valley residents will see two names on the ballot – Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel of District 45 and Dana Caruso, a former assistant principal.

The new redistricting lines for state Assembly District 46 let go of Studio City and North Hills territory, but the district still proves to be a socio-economically diverse palate of residents stretching from Van Nuys to Calabasas.

Voters have consecutively elected Democratic candidates to serve District 46. But Caruso, who is not related to mayoral candidate Rick Caruso, isn’t worried about making the primaries because she is the only Republican on the ballot. After June 7, it’s full speed ahead for her campaign team.

The candidates share similar interests in education, homelessness and the climate crisis but have different approaches. Caruso knows these issues are bipartisan and hopes that Republicans will be encouraged to vote in the primaries. She’s adamant about not giving up on Republican voters, saying there’s a chance to make a difference in this dominantly blue-hued state.

On education issues, Gabriel has steered legislation toward trying to make higher education affordable for all students. He knows that many students fall through the cracks because parents are struggling but their income isn’t quite low enough to qualify for help, and those students can end up couch-surfing or living in their cars as they try to get their degrees.

Caruso has a stronger gravitational pull to primary and secondary education with a 20-year track record working in LAUSD, starting off in the cafeterias, then becoming a math teacher and eventually an assistant principal at North Hollywood High School. “The motto at North Hollywood High was if you want the job done right then get Caruso to do it,” she said.

According to Caruso, public education has lost its focus. She sees students receiving a high-school diploma who go to college unprepared for college-level math or writing courses. She believes California’s decision to end the California High School Exit Exam has contributed to students’ low scores on state tests and she disagrees with placing college students in remedial courses, saying such students will feel overwhelmed and eventually drop out.  With that said, she’s eager to make legislative choices that she believes will rectify the losses in public education.

Gabriel and Caruso agree that the streets need to be safer. Gabriel cites patterns of hate-motivated violence in his communities targeted more toward the Asian Pacific Islander community because of the COVID-19 pandemic. He has also pursued efforts to protect Californians from gun violence. In February he introduced Assembly Bill 1929, which would provide Medi-Cal reimbursement for the Hospital-Based Violence Intervention Program, to expand funding for gun violence prevention efforts.

Caruso is a strong proponent of funding the police, especially in the school system. The Encino resident cited many times when she heard helicopters hovering over the area. And while working in the schools, administration and staff had to break up student fights. “We really have to get back to the business of education,” she said. “Our children deserve the best education possible and if you look at the ratings of a lot of the high schools a lot of the parents feel the schools aren’t safe,” she said.

Gabriel approaches his job as an assembly member like he does the parenting of his three children under the age of six, by giving things his close attention. He knows that residents from Canoga Park have diverse needs compared to residents from Calabasas.

“My responsibility is to serve everyone in my district,” said Gabriel. “I am really committed to make sure that California protects reproductive rights,” said Gabriel, especially considering the leaked draft opinion from Roe v. Wade. He serves on the Select Committee on Reproductive Health in the Assembly and received support from Planned Parenthood in his 2018 campaign for the legislature.

“Another huge priority is making sure that the Valley gets its fair share in transportation funding,” said Gabriel. He wants to make sure Los Angeles officials don’t leave out the San Fernando Valley when it comes to expanding measures for transportation services.

In terms of homelessness, both advocate for creating targeted approaches that intervene and prevent homelessness.

“We need to put our money into the mental health facilities to give these people a fighting chance. It’s a destruction of a workforce. They should be adding to society instead of living on the streets,” said Caruso.

Gabriel also looks to rent relief for tenants and landlords and creating affordable housing to stop homelessness before it starts. “We need more accountability on how the money is being spent in the community,” said Gabriel.

In terms of the climate crisis, they have different takes on possible solutions.

Caruso proposes to investigate ways to water plants with brown water and recommends studying other countries and their drought-tolerant moves that would help California, like turning the landscape back into a desert-scape.

“This is the desert,” Caruso said. “It’s green because we are watering it. Cutting and watering grass is an expense and it’s a waste on our resources.”

Gabriel remembers a few weeks after his 2018 election when the Woolsey Fire broke out  and schools in the Calabasas area were shutting down. He remembers the record 120-degree summer day in Woodland Hills too. For Gabriel, its important that wildfires get addressed immediately, because if not, some of California’s progress to renewable energy gets wiped out with a single fire crisis.

While Gabriel has the advantage of being endorsed by the California Democratic Party and the Sierra Club and feels fortunate for the support of essential workers, Caruso is relying on her community of supporters to keep her afloat. She’s a member of the L.A. Hispanic Republican club and goes on a radio show on Saturday nights from 8 to 10 p.m. where she talks about her campaign issues.

She’s thrilled that Rick Caruso’s mayoral candidacy has highlighted her name. She calls it divine intervention and hopes to meet with him to work on campaign strategies.

ASSEMBLY DISTRICT 40 RACE AT A GLANCE

THE DISTRICT: West San Fernando Valley including Van Nuys, Encino, Tarzana, Canoga Park, Woodland Hills and Calabasas.

THE RACE: One Democrat, one Republican.

Democrat Jesse Gabriel is endorsed by the California Democratic Party, Sierra Club California, California Teachers Association, California Labor Federation.

Republican Dana Caruso is endorsed by the Republican Party of Los Angeles County and Reseda Tarzana Republican Women Federated Group.

Jesse Gabriel: Contributions: $79,756.86; Expenditures: $111,946.16; Ending Cash: $1,508,938.11

Dana Caruso: No contributions or expenditures reported
